what we saw at the beginning:

that whoever does not stand by his word, He exacted payment from the generation of the Flood and from the generation

of the Dispersion. The generation of the Dispersion used speech to act

against the divine purpose. There is no greater profanation

of

speech than taking this unique gift

that HaShem gave to man and acting with it

against Him. So what did HaShem do? He took from them

speech, and since then no one understands one

another:

"A man will not hear his fellow's language." Speech is meant to connect the physical reality

with the spiritual reality. What did the people of the generation

of the Dispersion do? They used speech to sever the creation

from the Creator. And this is connected, I did not explain it here

now, but I told you that whoever wants to understand

the matter, what they wanted to do, what is "let us make for ourselves

a name," look at Rashi. Rashi brings

the Midrash: a tower with its top in the heavens. They wanted to go up to the heavens

and wage war with the Master of the world. "Let us make

a name for ourselves" means: we will set

our own purpose and not take into account what You want. And so

there was a rebellion here against HaShem through the power of speech.

What did HaShem do? He took from them the power of

speech. Whoever does not stand by his word is not fit to speak,

and HaShem exacts payment

from him. This gives a much deeper understanding of the concept of

vain speech. We know it from a very young age,

right? Since we began to speak, we never understood

what it means. And what I said here

now is still not the whole matter. If you wish, there are

other lessons that speak about the power of speech, about

the topic of lashon hara and so on. There things

are explained much more, but as regards

our subject, to understand this matter: speech

is a holy action of the soul in the body, intelligent speech,

in that a person thinks before he speaks. "The end of the deed is in the thought from the start," but rather the end of speech, or

more precisely the beginning of speech, is in the thought that precedes

it. Do not speak

nonsense; think before you speak. Many people

speak and afterward say to themselves, "Oh, why

did I say that? Why did I say it?" Or "I should

have said..." You must think before speaking, not afterward;

then it is already too late.

Now we saw that this is also connected to a person

and his fellow: whoever does not stand by his word. This speaks here about

merchants, business

dealings. One must stand by one's word. You said it, honor

the word. Give respect to speech, because otherwise you are belittling

something that is the essence of man. Man is defined

as the speaker. So when we speak, we must speak to the point;

it is forbidden to profane

speech. Our parashah speaks about non-trivial speech,

speech between man and HaShem: "When you vow

a vow to HaShem." You are not speaking between you and your friend, between you,

between ourselves; you take upon yourself

a commitment toward the Master of the

world. You must pay it, and do not delay, for why

should HaShem be angry at your deeds?

That is, there will be a price for it. Therefore

it is better not to vow at all.

You vowed? Understand what you have entered into: a commitment

that you must fulfill as quickly as possible

and at the highest level.

You were not obligated to bind yourself; you

were not obligated to vow. You vowed, you must fulfill.

Here there is

a shining of a spotlight on the power of

speech. Let us see for a moment what this

says: the speech of

man. I will read you a few

lines in which I summarized the main points:

in man's speech, which expresses his uniqueness among

creatures

and his likeness

to his Creator, right, HaShem. Okay, speech

by HaShem is different, but it is written many

times in the Torah, "HaShem spoke to Moses, saying."

The whole creation was said

through speech, for He said,

"Let there be," right? There is a blessing that I assume everyone knows:

"Blessed are You, HaShem our Elokeinu, King of the universe, by whose word all came to be."

"By the word of HaShem the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of His mouth," for He said "Let there be," and "Elokim said, Let there be,"

and there was. So man is similar. Now, of course, HaShem

has no body and no likeness of a body, and there there is no

spiritual action... here we speak about

divine speech by way of metaphor, in order to express this

in man. This is how HaShem acts; He is

not body and not matter, for matter is limited and HaShem

is unlimited. So what does it mean

that HaShem says that He speaks? "HaShem spoke

to Moses, saying," "by the word of HaShem the heavens were made"? This is not

literal, it is not literal in relation to the Master of the world,

for there is a difference between us and Elokim: we have a body

and He does not.

In any case, the very possibility of speech, that is,

thought that, when it becomes speech, creates reality,

at least on the part of the Master of the world,

the words of HaShem created reality; all came to be

by His word. So in this likeness, man in this respect

is similar to HaShem in man's speech,

which expresses his uniqueness among creatures,

an exclusivity
